The rider cancelled 181 s (3 min 1 s) after matching at 09:00:10 [F3], i.e. more than 3 minutes, so the $6.61 cancellation fee is chargeable under NS-4 and the fee on record is neither unpublished nor inflated (surge 1.0×) [F6][F7][NS-4]. The rider's own complaint admits she was held up upstairs and cancelled herself [F3], so the delay was rider-side.

The rider's case is built entirely on NS-1(iii) — a continuous wait of more than 3 minutes at the pickup [F2][F4][F5]. That test only applies where the driver cancels on a claimed no-show (NS-1/NS-2, reached via NS-0's `cancelled_by = driver` branch). Here the driver did not cancel; the rider did [F3]. NS-4, the branch that actually governs this case, sets only a rider-side clock and imposes no waiting requirement on the driver, so the short curb window (30 s cumulative inside 200 m, 11 s after the tap) does not by itself unlock a refund [F1][F2][F5][NS-1][NS-4]. The driver's statement claiming he waited 6+ minutes at the stand is a claim, not a chat record, and it conflicts with the recorded timeline; the system records (gps/timeline) prevail, so I do not rely on it — but since NS-1 is not engaged, the disbelieved statement removes nothing the driver needed [F8][F9][NS-1].

No safety issue arises: I read the complaint, the driver's statement and the record — there is no threat, intimidation, harassment or dangerous-driving allegation anywhere [F8][F9]. The record as it stands settles every element NS-0, NS-4 and NS-7 require (cancellation party, timing, fee amount, dispute window), so evidence is sufficient and no account flag is warranted: the "I'm Here" tap was inside the 200 m radius (39 m), so the NS-2 flag limb is not triggered, and the driver's clean profile means no RD-6/NS-2 action either [F5][F14][NS-2][NS-3][RD-6].

I therefore uphold the fee: NS-4 makes the $6.61 chargeable and no clause in the rider-cancellation branch waives it [F3][F6][F7][NS-4][NS-7].

what_would_change: Had the rider cancelled within 3 minutes of matching, NS-4 would have waived the $6.61 fee.

claims.assertion: The $6.61 cancellation fee charged on this trip is recorded at F6 and the rider cancelled the instant (RydeX) booking herself at 09:03:11, so the case is governed by the rider-cancellation rule for on-demand trips, NS-0/NS-4.

The rider cancelled 3 min 1 s after acceptance (accepted 09:00:10, cancelled 09:03:11), which is more than the 3-minute grace window in NS-4; on its face that makes the $6.61 fee chargeable, which is why the rider needs the fee reviewed against NS-1 rather than the grace period.

The driver did not satisfy the waiting requirement of NS-1(iii): after first coming within 200 m of the pickup at 09:02:40 he remained inside 200 m for only 30 s before the 09:03:11 cancellation, far short of the continuous 3 minutes (180 s) NS-1 requires; the fee therefore falls under NS-2 and must be refunded in full.

Measured from the driver's own 'I'm Here' tap at 09:03:00 he stayed within 200 m for only 11 s after the tap (F5; arrival within 200 m at 09:02:40 per F4, cancellation 31 s after recorded arrival), so even taking the tap as the starting point the 3-minute continuous wait of NS-1(iii) was never met.

Although the driver tapped 'I'm Here' while 39 m from the pickup point (within the 200 m arrival radius, so NS-2's flag_account limb is not triggered), the tap at 09:03:00 came only 11 s before the rider cancelled, leaving no time for the required wait; the GPS record wins over the driver's statement that he waited more than 6 minutes.

The record of arrival itself shows 09:02:40, only 31 s before cancellation (F4), so no reading of the timeline yields the 'more than 3 minutes waiting at the pickup' that NS-1(i)-(iii) requires; the fee of $6.61 on record (F6, no surge per F7) is therefore not chargeable and should be refunded in full.

There is no in-app chat in this case (F8), so there is no rider message consenting to anything, and the driver's post-trip statement (F9) is a claim only; the only admissible waiting evidence is the GPS/timeline record, which fails NS-1.

The dispute was filed promptly within the NS-7 30-day window and concerns only the $6.61 fee on record (F6), so the requested remedy is a full refund of that fee by voucher under NS-7; no account flag against the rider is warranted as nothing in the record supports one.

weaknesses: The rider's own complaint admits she was held up upstairs and cancelled herself 181 s after matching (F3), which is past the 3-minute grace window, so NS-4 on its face makes the fee chargeable and my client's story gives the driver a sympathetic narrative.

The driver did tap 'I'm Here' at 09:03:00 only 39 m from the pickup, i.e. inside the 200 m arrival radius (F5), so NS-1(i) and (ii) are satisfied and the other side will argue he was present and waiting; my case rests solely on the short duration in NS-1(iii) (30 s cumulative within 200 m per F2, 11 s after the tap per F5).
The rider's profile shows 3 disputes in 90 days with 0 upheld (F13), which the driver's side may use to suggest a pattern of fee disputes, even though profile facts cannot decide the case.

The driver's statement claims a wait of more than 6 minutes at the stand (F9); although it loses to the GPS/timeline records (F2, F4, F5), a human reviewer might weigh his 4.9 rating and 700 trips (F14) as credibility support.

claims.assertion: The rider cancelled the ride herself at 09:03:11, 3 min 1 s after matching at 09:00:10, and the $6.61 cancellation fee was recorded on that cancellation — this is a rider-cancellation case, so only NS-0/NS-4 govern it.

Because the cancellation came more than 3 minutes after matching (181 s, i.e. > 3:00), the $6.61 cancellation fee is payable under NS-4 and should stand; the rider's own account ('I was two minutes away… I got held up upstairs, gave up and cancelled') is an admission that the delay was hers, not the driver's.

The driver did everything the platform requires of him: the platform recorded his arrival at the pickup at 09:02:40 (39 m away at closest approach) and he tapped 'I'm Here' at 09:03:00 while 39 m from the pickup point — well within the 200 m arrival radius — so there is no basis to treat this as an abusive arrival tap.

The rider's complaint about 'still being charged' cannot rest on any driver-attributable delay: the driver was stationary at/near the pickup from 09:02:40 until the rider cancelled at 09:03:11, and no traffic incident, congestion band or weather condition on the route explains a driver-side failure to arrive earlier (Anson Road band 4 flows at 30–39 km/h; fair weather; no incidents).

The driver's written statement that he 'waited more than 6 minutes and called twice' (F9) is not corroborated by the timeline (31 s between recorded arrival and cancellation) and no in-app chat exists, so the fee is defended on the system record alone; the statement is only relevant as the driver's uncontradicted account that he was present and trying to reach the rider.

The driver's record is clean — 4.4 years on the platform, 4.9 rating, 700 trips in 90 days and 0 disputes upheld in 90 days — so no flag_account action is warranted against him, whereas the rider has 3 disputes in 90 days.

weaknesses: The shortest honest reading of the timeline cuts against the driver's own statement: F4 and F5 show the driver only entered the 200 m radius at 09:02:40 and stayed within it for 30 s (F2), 11 s after his 'I'm Here' tap, so he cannot satisfy NS-1(iii)'s continuous > 3 minutes of waiting at the pickup — the other side will say the driver never actually waited and cancelled-by-rider fee rests only on NS-4's clock, not on any service the driver rendered.

F5 records the arrival confirmation as a driver 'I'm Here' tap at 39 m from the pickup point; if the judge reads the driver's post-hoc claim of 'more than 6 minutes' waiting (F9) as inconsistent with the GPS record (F2, F4), the driver's credibility suffers and the rider can argue he was not at the pickup as required by NS-1(ii) at the relevant time.

The rider cancelled 181 s after matching by only 1 second over the threshold (F3); any finding that the matching timestamp or the cancellation time is off, or that the free-cancellation window should be excused, would erase the $6.61 entirely, and the driver has no GPS record of waiting at the stand before 09:02:40 to show he was not the cause of the 3-minute delay.

points.response: Conceded as to the gate: NS-0 routes a rider-cancelled on-demand booking to NS-4, and it is not in dispute that the rider cancelled at 09:03:11 with $6.61 on record (F3, F6). But NS-4 only sets the *rider-side* clock; it does not answer whether the driver earned the fee, and D1 stops before that question.

The rider's candour that she was held up upstairs (F3 window, 181 s) is not a licence for the driver to collect a fee he did not qualify for: the fee's driver-side preconditions live in NS-1, and the same system records that defeat them are the records the driver himself relies on.

Agreed that the 09:03:00 tap is not an abusive tap — 39 m is inside the 200 m radius (F5), so NS-2's flag_account limb is not triggered — but that concession is fatal to the driver's fee defence, because NS-1(iii) requires >3 continuous minutes inside 200 m and the record shows only 30 s cumulatively (F2) and 11 s after the tap (F5).

This actually concedes my case: with no incident, no congestion band and fair weather (F10, F11, F12) there is no 'reasonable cause' and nothing to explain the driver's late arrival, and his presence in the radius lasted only 30 s (F2) — the record shows no qualifying wait, not a driver-side excuse.

The driver's 'more than 6 minutes' claim (F9) is contradicted by F4 (recorded arrival 09:02:40, cancellation 31 s later) and by the absence of any in-app chat (F8), so under the system-record-wins rule it cannot supply the NS-1(iii) wait the timeline denies; uncorroborated presence is not a qualifying wait.

I do not seek flag_account against the driver — his clean profile (F14) and the in-radius tap (F5) mean no fraud finding — but the rider's profile (F13) cannot convert a fee that fails NS-1 into a payable one; profile facts may support an action, never the finding.
Agreed: the rider cancelled her own RydeX booking and the $6.61 fee is recorded on that cancellation (F3, F6), so the case runs on NS-0/NS-4 — which is exactly why the fee stands.
Accepted: 181 s after matching is past the 3-minute window, so NS-4 makes the fee chargeable (F3); NS-1 is the driver-cancellation branch and does not apply where the rider cancels.

NS-1(iii) governs a driver who cancels on a claimed no-show; here the rider cancelled (F3), so NS-1/NS-2 are not engaged and the fee is validated by the NS-4 clock rather than by how long the driver idled. The driver was nevertheless physically at the pickup from 09:02:40, 39 m away (F1, F4).

The 31-second curb window is irrelevant to liability on a rider cancellation: once the rider cancels past the 3-minute mark (F3), NS-4 charges the fee and imposes no 3-minute waiting requirement on the driver; that requirement exists only under NS-1(iii) for driver-cancelled no-shows.

Conceded as to the record: the driver's post-trip statement (F9) loses to GPS (F2, F4, F5), which shows 30 s inside 200 m and 11 s after the tap, so NS-1(iii) is not met. That does not help the rider here, because the applicable rule is NS-4 (F3) and the driver was present at the pickup when the rider cancelled.

The premise fails: NS-1(i)-(iii) is the test only where the driver cancels for no-show; the rider cancelled at 09:03:11 (F3), and NS-4 charges the $6.61 for exactly that, with no surge inflating it (F7).

Agreed there is no chat (F8) and that the driver's statement yields to the system record (F2, F4); that same record shows the driver within 200 m from 09:02:40 and 39 m from the pickup at 09:03:00 (F1, F4, F5), so he was on hand when the rider gave up.

The NS-7 30-day window and voucher form are not in dispute, but they apply only to a fee that should not have been charged; the $6.61 was validly charged under NS-4 (F3, F6), so neither a full nor a partial refund is due, and no flag against the driver's clean record is warranted (F14).
